content.p: On the hot morning of 1 August 1966, a 25-year-old student named Charles Whitman rode an elevator up the landmark tower of the University of Texas at Austin, pulling a footlocker of weapons behind him. At 11:48 a.m. he began shooting from the outdoor observation deck at people crossing the campus and the streets around it. For the next 96 minutes the university was a killing ground. The Texas State Historical Association counts seventeen dead, among them Whitman's wife and mother, whom he had killed hours earlier, and 31 people treated for wounds.

Whitman was shot dead on the deck at 1:24 p.m. by two Austin police officers. What followed has lasted far longer than the siege: a dispute over a tumour found in his brain, a rebuilding of how American police and campuses prepare for gunmen, and a memorial that the university took half a century to complete.

According to the Texas State Historical Association, the violence began in the early hours of the morning, when Whitman killed his mother, Margaret, at her apartment near downtown Austin. About three hours later he returned to his small house in south Austin and killed his wife, Kathleen, as she slept. Gary Lavergne, quoted by PBS, describes a man who was methodical: he placed his mother's body in bed as if she were sleeping, then went home and stabbed his wife. By three o'clock, Lavergne said, both women were dead. Lavergne is the author of the 1997 book A Sniper in the Tower.

From about 3:00 a.m. until he reached the campus around 11:30, the historical association says, Whitman wrote several notes and prepared for a long siege, buying and packing guns, about 700 rounds of ammunition and survivalist supplies. Lavergne told PBS that the rest of the night and morning went on polishing weapons and buying more ammunition, all toward the specific goal of going to the top of the tower and shooting people. In a note left on his wife's body, quoted by PBS, Whitman wrote: "I don't really understand myself these days." He described "many unusual and irrational thoughts" that "constantly recur".

Whitman wore overalls to pass as a janitor, the historical association says, and wheeled the footlocker on a two-wheeled dolly into the elevator and up to the twenty-seventh floor. The remaining climb, with his gear, was on foot: three flights of stairs to the twenty-eighth floor, which holds the reception area and the deck. His first victim on campus was a university employee who worked as the receptionist there.

Two tourists, a woman named Cheryl and her friend Don, were on the deck earlier that morning and walked back through the reception room as Whitman bent over a couch. Cheryl recalled in an oral history published by Spectrum News that Whitman stood up with a rifle in each hand, smiled, and asked how they were. They kept walking. Within about a minute, she said, a family from Texarkana came up the stairs and Whitman shot at them with a shotgun. According to the historical association, two members of the family died immediately and two others were badly wounded. The association says the shotgun had been illegally modified.

Whitman then went out onto the deck and blocked the door. The deck runs round the whole of the twenty-eighth floor, and the association notes that three openings in each outer wall, meant as rainspouts, worked as firing slits that protected him from shots returned from below.

The first people shot were on the South Mall, according to the Texas Tribune's report on the anniversary. Gary Lavergne told CBS Austin that the first victims were pretty clearly Claire Wilson and Thomas Eckman. Wilson was visibly pregnant, Lavergne said, and the first shot went through her womb. She recalled a "huge jolt", with her boyfriend asking what was wrong, before he was hit too. Lavergne said the second shot went through Eckman's back and killed him almost instantly. Wilson, now Claire Wilson James, lay on the concrete in the heat for about 90 minutes. She told CBS Austin that she remembered how blue the sky was and that doctors later gave her a 50 percent chance of surviving. She spent three months in hospital. She also lost her unborn baby.

Others on the ground described the same confusion. Neal Spelce, a reporter, said he heard the first radio call about shots on the campus and drove to the scene. On the air he told people to stay away. He said a policeman, Billy Speed, had been shot and killed, and that a boy on a bicycle was hit as he rode. A student, Artly Snuff, recalled that students went home for deer rifles and fired at the tower. The Tribune's essay says the officers who finally closed in had to move slowly partly because of nearly constant fire from citizens with hunting rifles on the ground. Spelce said the citizens did not hit the gunman but helped keep him pinned down. In the same account Snuff said he thought most of the shooting victims were hit in the first 10 to 15 minutes.

Nothing like it had happened before, Spelce said. There was no way to call it a school shooting, because there had never been one. Emergency medical services did not exist in their later form: Spelce said funeral homes were dispatching ambulances.

Snuff described how he and a classmate, James Love, ran onto the mall to carry Wilson to cover, after about an hour of her lying exposed. A young woman, whom Snuff named as Rita Starpattern, had run out and lain beside Wilson, talking to her to keep her awake, for about an hour and a half.

Ramiro "Ray" Martinez was an off-duty Austin officer who had been polishing his uniform for a 3 p.m. shift when he heard the news, according to his account in the Spectrum News oral history. He phoned the station, was told they needed help, put on his uniform and drove in. He crossed the campus by sheltering behind buildings and trees and rode the elevator toward the top. On the upper floors he found officer Jerry Day and a civilian, Allen Crum, a University Co-op employee, who insisted on going up with him. Martinez said he told Crum to "consider yourself deputized".

Martinez described the wounded on the first landing he reached, among them a dead boy and his aunt, and a severely wounded woman. A survivor of the Texarkana family, Mr Gabour, was brought down in the elevator and asked for a gun. Martinez said he and Day had to restrain him.

The historical association's summary of the ending is that two uniformed Austin patrol officers, Martinez and Houston McCoy, ambushed Whitman on the northwest corner of the deck at 1:24 p.m. It says Crum had gone to the deck with Martinez and waited near the south doorway, and that, according to Crum's statement to police, officer Jerry Day was also at the door. Martinez himself said he first had to push a dolly out of the way at the door. The Tribune's essay says McCoy had a shotgun and arrived with Martinez and Crum at the observatory. A young wounded man on the way up had reached for McCoy's shotgun and said he wanted to shoot the gunman, and McCoy answered that he would do it for him. In the Tribune's telling, the two officers edged around a corner, opened fire, and Whitman slumped dead.
At the 2016 anniversary, ABC News reported that the university's president recognised seven officers who went up the tower. Three of them had died by then and four attended.

The number of dead is given differently by different outlets, and the difference is partly one of timing and partly of what is counted. The historical association says seventeen died including Whitman's wife and mother: fifteen on 1 August, including Officer Speed, another on 8 August, and a final victim in 2001 of a gunshot-related wound. ABC News also reported 17 dead. The Texas Tribune's ceremony report spoke of 16 people killed, and PBS said 16 killed and more than 30 wounded in one place, then 16 dead and 32 wounded elsewhere in the same piece. The Daily Texan wrote that Whitman killed 13 people on campus; it corrected an earlier version of that story that said 14. The Tribune's 2022 essay says eleven were dead on the ground, with three killed inside the tower, and refers to the wife and 15 other innocent people.

The Daily Texan says Whitman's suicide note requested an autopsy, since he expected it to reveal a "visible physical disorder". The Daily Texan describes a tumour between the thalamus, hypothalamus and amygdala that had grown to about the size of a pecan. PBS reports that one doctor called the "grayish yellow mass" irrelevant to the shooting, but a later medical panel diagnosed it as a glioblastoma and said it might have played a part in his loss of control over his feelings and behaviour. Dr Stuart Brown of Baylor College of Medicine wrote in the 1966 report that the "highly malignant brain tumor conceivably could have contributed".

The panel was part of the commission formed by Governor John Connally immediately after the shooting. The historical association says the 32-member group of mental health and other medical experts examined every aspect of the case and could not positively identify a cause for the rampage.

Fifty years later, experts still did not agree. Michael Koenigs, an expert on brain lesions, told the Daily Texan that the tumour's position against the amygdala could have affected Whitman's mental state, though it was unlikely to have caused a psychotic rage by itself. N. Bradley Keele, who studies the amygdala, thought the tumour was unlikely to be the sole or an important cause, pointing to what he called a very abusive home and to Whitman's admitted violence towards his wife. Lavergne said Whitman made a series of correct decisions toward a goal over 48 hours, and he told the paper he doubted the tumour's existence after meeting two doctors who did not believe in it. The Daily Texan added that Whitman's brain has been reported by some media outlets as one of the "missing" brains UT employees disposed of in 2002, which, if true, would leave no brain to scan.
The Tribune essay goes further, saying that although he did have a tumour, it has never been conclusively proven that it led him to plan and carry out the attack.

PBS reports that six months before the shooting Whitman went to a school psychiatrist and admitted imagining himself on the tower with a deer rifle, shooting people. Lavergne said the psychiatrist, Dr Maurice D. Heatly, claimed that many students described violent fantasies. Heatly told reporters after the shooting that students at the clinic commonly pointed to the tower as the place for a desperate act, and that Whitman had no psychosis symptoms. Whitman never went back to the clinic. PBS also noted that Whitman did not mention that he had been abusing amphetamines.

Lavergne told PBS that Whitman, a former Marine and Eagle Scout, did not have serious mental illness, only common problems like depression and anxiety, and that he was manipulative, leaving a good impression despite a 1.9 grade point average and the assault of his wife. The Tribune's essay describes his father as rigid and authoritarian, and says his parents' marriage had fallen apart a few months earlier.

The historical association calls the shooting a seminal event in American law enforcement. Austin's officers, it says, had no tactical training, clear communication, adequate weapons or unified command. Along with the 1965 Watts riots, the shooting is often cited as a precursor of police SWAT teams. In 1967 the Texas legislature passed Senate Bill 162, which Governor Connally signed on 27 April, allowing higher education institutions to have their own police forces. It led to the University of Texas Police Department, which replaced a service of unarmed watchmen who handled traffic and parking. The commission's suggestion to expand counselling led to the replacement of the Student Health Center's "mental hygiene clinic" with what became the UT Counseling and Mental Health Center.

The observation deck was closed for several months for repairs. Four people took their own lives from the deck between 1968 and 1974, after three in the building's first thirty years. The twenty-eighth floor closed in 1974 and the regents voted in February 1976 to close the deck for good. It reopened to the public after the 1999 Tower Memorial Garden dedication, with the deck enclosed by a mesh of stainless steel bars.

The university's first memorial to the dead came only on 1 August 1999 with the Tower Garden, just north of the tower. A plaque on a boulder was added in 2007 without any victims' names. On 1 August 2016, the fiftieth anniversary, a monument of Texas pink granite carrying the engraved names of the seventeen victims was dedicated.

The ceremony began on the South Mall, where the first victims fell. The tower clock was stopped at 11:48 a.m. for 24 hours, and a bagpiper led the crowd to the garden. The student body presidents of 1966 and 2016 took turns reading the names, and the tower bell tolled after each. According to the Texas Tribune, nobody spoke Whitman's name. President Gregory Fenves called the memorial "long, long overdue" and said survivors had not received the support they needed. James Bryce, a student in 1966, said that afterwards the school scrubbed the sidewalks, put in new windows and tried to "get back to normal". Claire Wilson James, who received a standing ovation alongside Martinez, asked the crowd to treasure "the ones we walk with each moment".

The same day, a Texas law took effect letting concealed handgun licence holders carry guns into public university buildings. Gregory Vincent, the university's vice president for diversity and community engagement, told ABC News it was "a most unfortunate coincidence".
